---
title: "Unsafe Rust and FFI: Who Proves Safety?"
description: "One Rust language concept taught with one short runnable example and a precise explanation."
---

## The question

**Does `unsafe` turn off the entire Rust type system?**

No. Unsafe allows a small set of operations such as dereferencing raw pointers or calling unsafe functions. It transfers the proof obligation for those operations to the programmer; safe callers may still depend on those guarantees.

## The rule to remember

Use safe references whenever possible; create narrow `unsafe` blocks only when low-level work requires them.

## The smallest complete example

Paste into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`. The [Rust examples page](examples/index.qmd) describes how to check all snippets automatically.

~~~rust
fn main() {
    let mut n = 3;
    let ptr: *mut i32 = &mut n;
    unsafe { *ptr += 1; }
    println!("{n}"); // 4
}
~~~

**Follow the state:** A raw pointer is created from a live mutable reference. Dereferencing it requires `unsafe`. Here `n` remains valid throughout, and there is no conflicting pointer access. The `unsafe` block marks an operation the compiler cannot fully validate.

## Important limitation

This simple example does NOT need unsafe in real code: `n += 1` is clearer and safer. Invalid raw pointers, aliasing violations or data races can create undefined behaviour even if the code compiles.
